The group successfully delivered the SG60 Baby Gift project during the financial year. 
Despite this, revenue declined by 1.2% to $17.39 million from $17.60 million in FY2025, 
while gross profit fell by 3.5%, or approximately $0.31 million, to $8.54 million. 
 
Profit attributable to shareholders increased to $0.36 million, from $0.26 million in FY2025, 
driven primarily by a 12.6% reduction in administrative expenses, equivalent to 
approximately $0.93 million including lower staff costs (of $0.74 million), and a $0.26 million 
write-back of expected credit loss allowances. 
 
(i) 
Given the decline in revenue and the reduction in headcount from 114 to 95 
employees, what is the group’s target operating model for the Gifts 
segment? Can management quantify how much of the headcount reduction 
came from improved productivity, automation or removal of excess 
capacity, as opposed to lower business volumes? What specific growth 
initiatives does the group have going forward?   
 
(ii) 
How is the group applying artificial intelligence across its business, beyond 
general exploration or experimentation? Which specific processes or 
customer-facing activities are being targeted, and what measurable benefits 
have been realised in areas such as labour productivity, operating costs, 
sales conversion or customer experience? 
 
The group is modernising its legacy enterprise resource planning (ERP) system to improve 
operational efficiency and financial governance. It also migrated its e-commerce platform to 
Shopify to enhance cybersecurity, streamline operations and improve the online shopping 
experience. 
 
(iii) 
What is the expected completion date and total cost of the ERP 
modernisation? What annual cost savings are expected from the ERP 
modernisation and Shopify migration projects?  
 
(iv) 
Following the migration to Shopify, what improvements have been 
observed in website conversion rates, online sales, fulfilment efficiency, 
cybersecurity and operating costs?

The group acquired a 3,301 sqm freehold land parcel at Jalan Jamal and Elite Park 
Avenue for $39.5 million on 18 March 2025. In its FY2025 annual report, management 
indicated that work would commence in 2026 to develop up to ten three-storey landed 
residential units. 
 
In the FY2026 annual report, the development plans were revised to comprise six semi-
detached houses and three detached houses, each designed as a three-storey residence with 
an attic, private swimming pool and basement car park. The group has appointed a main 
contractor and is preparing to launch the development in the first half of 2027, with 
construction targeted to commence in the fourth quarter of 2026. 

(i) 
Given that the land was acquired in March 2025 and sales are expected to 
launch only in the first half of 2027, what are the main factors driving this 
two-year timeline? Has management encountered any unexpected delays, 
and if so, what additional holding costs and execution risks have arisen as a 
result? 
 
(ii) 
How has management assessed demand and buyer affordability for this 
specific mix of semi-detached and detached homes, and how will it 
determine launch prices to optimise profitability without compromising 
sales velocity?  
 
(iii) 
Was the main contractor appointed under a fixed-price contract? If not, how 
does management intend to manage construction cost inflation and protect 
the project's target margin?

The group reported an 81% increase in net profit to $22.7 million in FY2026, compared 
to $12.5 million in FY2025. However, net cash used in operating activities increased to 
$(15.52) million from $(11.37) million. Trade receivables also rose from $75.9 million to 
$117.9 million as at 30 June 2026, with the increase largely attributable to a $41.9 million 
rise in pawnshop loans. 
 
(Adapted from company annual report) 
 
(i) 
What is the current outstanding balance of pawnshop loans, and how much 
further growth can the group accommodate within its existing capital and 
liquidity position? For the non-pawnbroking trade receivable balances, how 
has the ageing profile changed? 
 
Net debt increased by $28.8 million to $94.9 million in FY2026, with net debt to equity rising 
from 46.8% to 58.4%. 
 
 
(Source: company annual report; additional calculation by SIAS) 

(ii) 
What gearing or net debt limits has the board established? Has management 
stress-tested the group's ability to service its debt and meet working capital 
requirements under scenarios involving slower receivables collection, 
lower gold prices, weaker jewellery sales or a contraction in pawnbroking 
activity?
qa.answer:
The group reported an 81% increase in net profit to $22.7 million in FY2026, compared to $12.5 
million in FY2025. However, net cash used in operating activities increased to $(15.52) million 
from $(11.37) million. Trade receivables also rose from $75.9 million to $117.9 million as at 30 
June 2026, with the increase largely attributable to a $41.9 million rise in pawnshop loans. 
 
 
(Adapted from company annual report) 
 
(i) What is the current outstanding balance of pawnshop loans, and how much further growth 
can the group accommodate within its existing capital and liquidity position? For the non-
pawnbroking trade receivable balances, how has the ageing profile changed? 
 
As disclosed in Note 28(a) to the audited financial statements, the outstanding balance of financial 
services receivables as at 30 June 2026 was $93.7 million. Financial services receivables consist 
substantially of pawnshop loans, while other secured lending is insignificant as at 30 June 2026. 
 
The Group’s existing banking facilities are sufficient to support its current business plans. 
Management will continue to assess funding capacity and liquidity before pursuing further growth. 
 
The non-pawnbroking trade receivable balances relate primarily to that of the “wholesale and 
exhibitions jewellery business”. The ageing profile of these trade receivable balances as at 30 June 
2025 and 2026 has been summarised in the table in Question 2 below.  

Net debt increased by $28.8 million to $94.9 million in FY2026, with net debt to equity rising from 
46.8% to 58.4%. 
 
 
(Source: company annual report; additional calculation by SIAS) 
 
(ii) What gearing or net debt limits has the board established? Has management stress-tested 
the group's ability to service its debt and meet working capital requirements under scenarios 
involving slower receivables collection, lower gold prices, weaker jewellery sales or a 
contraction in pawnbroking activity? 
 
The Group monitors gearing using the measure disclosed in Note 30 to the audited financial 
statements, namely net debt as a proportion of total capital, where total capital refers to the sum of 
net debt and equity attributable to the owners of the Company. This ratio increased from 31.9% to 
36.9% in FY2026. Using the net-debt-to-equity measure calculated by SIAS, the ratio increased 
from 46.8% to 58.4% over the same period. Both measures reflect the same $28.8 million increase 
in net debt, which was mainly used to fund the growth of the pawnbroking loan book. 
 
Management closely monitors the Group’s cash flow position and prepares regular cash flow 
forecasts and plans to assess funding and working capital requirements. These forecasts take into 
account the Group’s foreseeable and probable scenarios. The Group will also continue to monitor 
its gearing, debt-servicing capacity and overall financial position as its borrowing requirements 
evolve

qa.answer:
The “allowance for impairment of trade receivables from the group’s wholesale and exhibition 
jewellery business” is a key audit matter1 (KAM) highlighted by the independent auditors in their 
report on the audit of the financial statements. As noted in the KAM, these trade receivables are 
significant to the group, representing 7% of total assets as at year end. 
 
The credit risk exposure on the group’s trade receivables from the group’s jewellery business 
using provision matrix is shown below. 

(Source: company annual report) 
 
Note: 1 Key audit matters are those matters that, in the professional judgement of the Independent 
Auditor, were of most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period. 
 
(i) What are the profiles of the customers with overdue trade receivable balances? What 
recovery actions has management taken? Has the board assessed whether customer credit 
assessment, credit limits, payment terms or ongoing monitoring could be strengthened?  
 
The overdue trade receivables balances arose mainly from the Group’s wholesale and exhibition 
jewellery business and included customers in Asia, West Asia and America. The older balances are 
substantially provided for as shown in the table above. Of the $5.9 million outstanding for more than 
three years, $5.4 million has been provided for impairment. Of the $2.3 million outstanding for one 
to three years, $1.7 million has been provided for impairment. 
 
As disclosed in Note 28(a) to the audited financial statements, the Group applies the simplified 
approach and recognises a loss allowance based on lifetime expected credit losses (ECLs) at each 
reporting date. Trade receivables that are credit impaired are assessed for impairment by making 
debtor-specific assessment. The ECL model considers the Group’s assessment of the collectability, 
analysis of historical analysis and credit losses, and aging analysis of trade receivables.  
 
Notably, trade receivables from the wholesale and exhibition segment rose 27% while segment 
revenue rose 50%. This improvement reflects the Group’s efforts to strengthen credit control.  
 
Management continues to review the effectiveness of these controls and will implement 
enhancements where appropriate to strengthen collection efforts and mitigate credit risk. 
 
Separately, the group also wrote off $1.07 million of inventory during FY2026.  
(ii) What were the main reasons for the $1.07 million inventory write-offs in FY2026, and which 
product categories accounted for the largest amounts? What changes has management 
made to inventory purchasing, ageing reviews and stock controls to reduce the risk of 
further write-offs?  
 
The $1.07 million write-off of obsolete stock arose from the Group’s inventory review, which took 
into account the physical condition and commercial value of stock, prevailing market conditions, 
current and expected demand, and the costs of reworking the inventory. 
 
The $1.07 million write-off was relatively small compared with the Group’s total inventory balance 
of $138 million, representing approximately 0.8% as at 30 June 2026. 
 
Management continues to monitor inventory condition, aging and movements through its existing 
inventory controls and review processes

qa.answer:
On 2 October 2026, the company announced the appointment of Novus Corporate Finance Pte. 
Ltd. as its new continuing sponsor, replacing PrimePartners Corporate Finance Pte. Ltd., with 
effect from 4 October 2026. The company attributed the change to “commercial reasons”.  
 
(i) Could the independent directors explain the specific reasons for changing sponsors, 
beyond the stated “commercial reasons”? Did the board identify any new focus areas or new 
requirements that prompted the change, and what improvements does it expect from the 
new continuing sponsor?  
 
The previous continuing sponsor has served the Company for more than 10 years, since the 
Company’s listing on Catalist.  The Independent Directors note that the change in continuing 
sponsor followed the Board’s periodic review of the Company’s sponsorship arrangements as part 
of its ordinary governance processes. In considering the length of the previous continuing sponsor’s 
tenure, the Company’s business, scale, and strategic priorities, the Board concluded that the 
appointment of Novus Corporate Finance Pte. Ltd. (“Novus”) was appropriate for the Company’s 
current needs and next phase of development. 
 
The Board welcomes Novus as the Company’s continuing sponsor and expects it to provide ongoing 
guidance on Catalist-rule compliance, corporate governance and disclosure obligations.   
 
(ii) What criteria did the board use to evaluate potential replacement sponsors, and what factors 
distinguished Novus from the alternatives considered?  
 
In evaluating eligible Catalist sponsors, the Board considered each firm’s track record, its 
experience with issuers of comparable size and sector, the composition of the proposed 
engagement team, its capital markets capability and the fees proposed. Following consideration of 
the available options and assessment of eligible Catalist sponsors, the Board concluded that the 
appointment of Novus is in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders. 
 
(iii) Does the board intend to pursue a transfer from Catalist to the SGX Mainboard? If so, what 
are the principal eligibility requirements the company has yet to meet, and what milestones 
and timeframe has management established to achieve them?  
 
The Company will make the appropriate announcement in accordance with the Catalist Rules 
should it pursue a transfer from Catalist to the SGX Mainboard.
